It’s time to prosecute climate crimes – with laws that already exist

Aaron Regunberg





Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct





The sky outside is hazy orange, and my five-year-old son is screaming bloody murder. “Sorry, buddy, we have to stay inside,” I say. “It’s not safe to breathe out there.” I had told him we’d be going to the beach today. Something inside me tears a little as I wonder how many promises he’ll see similarly broken in the coming years.
Far too many parents were forced to have some version of this conversation with their children this month, as smoke from record-breaking wildfires poured across the midwest and north-east. Some of them already had to tell their kids that their Fourth of July festivities were canceled because of the lethal heatwave that caused numerous mass casualty events earlier this month.

According to scientists, these extreme weather events are not “natural” disasters. A team of researchers already published a study finding that the Fourth of July heat wave would have been “virtually impossible” but for the climate crisis. Other studies – using methods recently validated by the National Academy of Sciences, the country’s top scientific advisory body – found that the pollution from individual big oil companies such as ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell and BP made some past climate-exacerbated heatwaves at least 10,000 times more likely compared with preindustrial levels.






The Guardian view on extreme heat: as risks escalate, adaptation plans are dangerously lagging | Editorial

Read more
Big oil’s role in these disasters was no accident. Decades ago, these companies were predicting that their fossil fuels would cause, in their own words, “globally catastrophic” climate harms that would create “more violent weather” and cause “suffering and death due to thermal extremes”. Even as they used this knowledge to protect their own infrastructure, they orchestrated fraudulent campaigns of climate denial and deception to lock us into the disasters we are currently experiencing.
It’s no wonder, then, that climate harms are increasingly being interpreted not just as tragedies but as crimes. “We need Nuremberg trials for Big Oil,” wrote one climate advocacy group in a recent post that received tens of thousands of likes – and the sentiment has been echoed by many others.

“For investors, a very strong El Niño should be viewed as a source of market dispersion rather than a uniformly negative shock,” says the research note.

articles.title: Hebridean salt marsh shows sea level changes over last 2,500 years
articles.raw_rss: Scientists said the relative sea level at Gress on the Isle of Lewis has risen by 1.2m over the last 2,500 years.
articles.raw_meta: Scientists said the relative sea level at Gress on the Isle of Lewis has risen by 1.2m over the last 2,500 years.
articles.jina_text:
A salt marsh in the Outer Hebrides provides an “almost unbroken record” of sea level changes over the last 2,500 years, scientists have said.




Researchers studying the marsh at Gress on the Isle of Lewis had originally been searching for deposits left by the Storegga tsunami, a massive wave triggered by an underwater landslide off Norway around 8,200 years ago.








Instead they were surprised to uncover 2,500 years of geological history preserved less than two metres beneath the surface, recording how sea levels have changed since around 500 BC.




They said the findings provide one of the most detailed records yet of how Scotland’s coastlines have responded to shifting climates and changes in the elevation of land since the end of the last Ice Age.




Dr Uisdean Nicholson, a sedimentary geologist from Heriot-Watt University’s School of Energy, Geoscience, Infrastructure and Society, said: “Salt marshes are incredibly sensitive to changes in sea level, so they preserve a detailed history of how coastlines evolve over time.




“And this one at Gress turned out to hold an almost unbroken record of the past 2,500 years.




“It’s amazing to get a snapshot of what the environment was like so far back in time, when the Persian empire was at its greatest extent and the Roman Republic was just getting started.”


The team analysed sediment cores taken from the marsh (Sue Dawson/PA)





The team took sediment cores from the marsh, which is located on the east coast of Lewis, and examined the microscopic algae and ancient plant remains layer by layer.











They said the analysis indicates the relative sea level at Gress has risen by around 1.2 metres over the past 2,500 years, with the rate of rise beginning to accelerate slightly around AD 950.




Professor Natasha Barlow, a coastal consultant at engineering consulting firm Haskoning, said, “Our results show that there is little or no ongoing land uplift following the melting of the British Irish ice sheet around 20,000 years ago on Lewis.







“Rather, sea level rise over the last 2,000 years is due to ongoing ice melt and warming of the ocean.”




Professor Sue Dawson, an expert on geohazards from Geography at the University of Dundee, said: “This painstaking work gives us an understanding of the way the rising and falling sea level has influenced the vegetation and the algae that grow and live in our coastal environments, which helps to unlock the sea level story”.

A planned solar panel installation proposed to be installed on what is believed to be a greenfield site has drawn criticism.
If approved, the installation in St Sampson would see 72 ground-mounted panels on agricultural land which has had no previous permanent construction on it. 
Critics said the choice of site was inappropriate because of wildlife concerns, and that the roof of the applicant's house beside the proposed site would possibly be more suitable. 
The applicant told the BBC he disputed it was a greenfield site and there had been greenhouses on the land which were later destroyed and buried. No decision date is currently set.


Chris Chadwick is a "huge fan" of renewable energy, but not on greenfield sites

He said he was "all for" renewable energy sites "but not at the expense of covering the greenfield sites".
"They've got a very large house there that they could put solar panels on the roof."

However, applicant L Shephard told the BBC he disputed the area was a greenfield site.

articles.title: Spain and France brace for new heatwaves as wildfire closes in on Bordeaux
articles.raw_rss: Temperatures are expected to soar past 40C in some regions as a heatwave builds, further hampering firefighting efforts.
articles.raw_meta: Temperatures are expected to soar past 40C in some regions as a heatwave builds, further hampering firefighting efforts.
articles.jina_text:
Firefighters in France's Gironde region face an "unprecedented" situation as they battle a blaze that "has a life of its own", the interior minister warns


ByJaroslav Lukiv and Yang Tian







27 July 2026
Updated 4 hours ago




Spain and France are bracing for new heatwaves with temperatures expected to soar past 40C in some regions.
Spain's national weather service says the severe weather is forecast to last until "at least" Sunday, and warns of "extreme" fire risks as firefighters continue to battle the some of the worst blazes in the country's history.
France's south-west regions Gironde and Landes are under "yellow alert" for a heatwave expected to peak on Wednesday, further hampering efforts to contain "very unpredictable" blazes in Gironde.
The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is preparing for "all eventualities", as one of the wildfires burning in France is 15km (nine miles) from the south-western city.
"We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered," said Thomas Cazenave. 
Some 220,000 people have been evacuated in France and more than 100,000 in Spain, where fires are burning "uncontrolled" west of Madrid.
President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, said the country was facing a "completely unprecedented wildfire" - the "toughest since World War Two".
Macron said a smaller fire in the Landes region had been contained, but the fight continued in neighbouring Gironde. 
While firefighters had made progress on Monday, Macron warned that "temperatures are set to rise again, the wind is still present, and therefore we must remain humble".
Earlier, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said the fire "has a life of its own".
Jerome Steffe, the mayor of Cestas, a town south of Bordeaux, told the BBC this "will be the fire of the century".
He described how 17,000 residents were evacuated from his town during the night when the fire swelled two days ago. So far, he said, the region has seen 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) of land burned and 240 houses destroyed.
"In my city the situation is really catastrophic," he added.
And although the fire is no longer moving as quickly, he said his teams have "won only a small battle" and emphasised that the risk remains from flying embers or a sudden change in wind direction.
"We put all our energy into creating protective firebreaks," he explained, but admitted "we are all scared in front of this situation."
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned the country "is going through an unprecedented fire season", with 116,085 hectares (286,852 acres) burned and 13,566 fire starts recorded since January.
The minister revealed in a post on X that nine out of 10 fires "are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution".
But he also said that not all these fires are accidents and some are deliberately set, adding that since 6 July, 162 arrests have taken place.

The Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new reality

Editorial





At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised





A new and ominous word has entered the vocabulary of firefighters struggling to cope with the vast wildfire sweeping through south-west France. A pyrocumulonimbus is a fire-generated thunderstorm that can whip up winds in unpredictable ways, making the containment of a blaze and assessment of its likely course far more difficult. A known phenomenon in North America and Australia, firefighters believe France is suffering its first in the Bordeaux region, as the country endures the consequences of the third major heatwave of the summer and prepares for a fourth.
The dire statistics of the ongoing fires in France and Spain tell a story of deepening devastation and human misery. A far greater expanse of French land has already been burnt this year, compared with the 30,000 hectares during the whole of 2025, while 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the Gironde. In Spain, the environment ministry has calculated that over 170,000 hectares have been affected, compared with 29,000 last year. Over 100,000 people have been forced to flee.



View image in fullscreen
Pedro Sánchez greeting emergency service workers. Photograph: Eva Manez/Reuters
As climate scientists long warned would be the case, Europe’s wildfires are worsening in intensity, scale and duration as the planet heats up. When the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attributed the current crisis to the effects of the climate emergency, he was stating the obvious. But to his great credit, Mr Sánchez has been among the few leaders to argue that the European Union’s green transition should be accelerated accordingly. Whether on funding adaptation efforts, or driving the macro changes needed to slow the rate of global heating, far too many others appear happy to fiddle while the continent burns.
In June, for example, with spectacularly bad timing, Emmanuel Macron’s government sought savings by announcing steep cuts to a Green Fund designed to help local authorities address climate and environmental challenges. Across Europe more generally, amid persistent low growth and the fallout from Donald Trump’s war on Iran, a false dichotomy is increasingly being drawn between green ambition and competitiveness. articles.jina_text:
Aid agencies have called on prime minister Andy Burnham to address drivers of inequality, injustice and poverty following the decision to reallocate international aid to help fight the climate crisis towards funding a cap on UK bus fares. 
The heads of 98 organisations, including Oxfam GB, WaterAid and ActionAid UK, have warned that countries already trapped in unfair debt cycles could be left with few choices but to borrow more to address the climate crisis. They highlighted that the crisis is not of their making.
“Politicians must stop pitting the needs of the British public against the needs of people in the majority World by raiding the already diminished UK aid budget to fund domestic spending,” the joint statement said. “Both face many of the same underlying challenges.”





The prime minister announced last week that he would change international climate donations into repayable loans to reduce the fare cap from £3 a journey to £2 next year. Around £400 million is expected to go towards the initiative by replacing international climate finance grants with loans, allowing the government to borrow more without violating its borrowing rules. 
Charities have said that the world’s most vulnerable people will be put at risk by the decision.

From BBC drama The Rapture on the climate crisis to Apple’s Criminal Record on the rise of the far right, culture often sees what politics fails to





In the BBC’s new apocalypse drama, The Rapture, the UK is engulfed in a terrifying heatwave. I watched a preview of the programme in May, while preparing to interview the lead actor Ruth Madeley. I thought at the time: “This will be much more frightening when it chimes with the real life weather, bad luck for them that it’s not coming out for a couple of months.” But, by the time of meeting Madeley the following month, we were already in the middle of a heatwave that would lead to the highest ever recorded June temperature in the UK. The whole encounter made the show feel even more prophetic. She was in a central London hotel, air-conditioned inside, but all the door handles and surrounding street furniture – benches segmented by metal arm rests, to make life just that little bit harder for homeless people – had got way too hot. It was like playing The Floor is Lava, except instead of “floor”, “everything”. It surely can’t hit the screens at a more apposite time than this, I thought, failing to predict that by late July we’d be in heatwave number three, and France would be on fire.






The Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better time







Read more

The Daily Mail’s reviewer was upset that Christianity was portrayed “as a bastion of anti-science nutjobs and fundamentalists” in the show, wondering rhetorically whether the BBC would ever create such a drama about a “Muslim imam”. Peculiar thing to get upset about, I thought, since the religion is really more of a symptom of, or even a garnish to, the central atmosphere of engulfing heat. It’s like complaining that cats get a bad rap in the 1974 film The Towering Inferno (yes, there is a cat in it).
TV puts a particular pressure on itself to describe the world it lands in, even when a show is developed at least a couple of years before. Often, the safe way to play it with surrounding factors – weather, politics, fashion – is to keep things so general that they could be any time this century. Every so often something will land that relates so tightly to current events, you forget to admire its foresight and just assume it was written yesterday. Season two of Criminal Record (Apple TV), the police drama, which Peter Capaldi lifts so far above procedural you forget the police even have procedures, opens with a little demo outside the Ministry of Defence. It turns deadly after the far right smashes through a lackadaisical police cordon that thought it was just there to deal with a bunch of peaceniks. It felt extremely 2026, yet it was conceived before violent far-right protests were a regular news event – before the riots after the the Southport attack, before asylum seeker hotels being set alight, before Elon Musk started talking about the inevitability of civil war in the UK. PM urged to uphold climate pledges made as mayor and ban new North Sea oil drilling


Experts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwaves




Leading climate scientists who created Greater Manchester’s carbon neutral by 2038 commitment are urging Andy Burnham to unequivocally reject new drilling in the North Sea.
In a letter to the prime minister they said he, as mayor of Greater Manchester, had unveiled one of the UK’s most ambitious local climate programmes that tackled housing, green growth and public transport.

Reports over the weekend continued to suggest Burnham was set to give the green light to controversial new drilling in the North Sea by approving the Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields, which were given approval under the Conservatives but put on hold by legal action. The ruling in court said a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact was required to take into account the effect on the climate of burning any fossil fuels extracted.


Prof Kevin Anderson and scientists from the Tyndall Centre at the School of Engineering at the University of Manchester, who wrote the open letter to the prime minister, said it was “with considerable concern” that they had read reports suggesting his government intended to approve the further development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields.
To do so would send a signal around the world that the UK was backtracking on its international climate commitments, they said.







Burnham risks Labour backlash if he reverses ban on new oil and gas drilling

Read more
If the reports were accurate that he intended to give the go ahead to drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank, the scientists wrote, “they represent a profound departure from the principles you promoted as Mayor of Greater Manchester”.
Labour made a manifesto promise that no new oil and gas licences would be issued, but Jackdaw and Rosebank were already in the system at the time of the last general election. A consultation on Jackdaw will finish on 8 August.
With extreme heat and wildfires across the UK and Europe this summer, the academics said the evidence showed global emissions must be cut by 8% every year if the world was to meet the upper limit of a maximum of 2C of heating in the Paris climate agreement.


Anderson and his colleagues urged Burnham to adhere to commitments he made when announcing the Greater Manchester carbon neutral by 2038 policy.

articles.title: Sir Ian Wood: North Sea oil tycoon and philanthropist dies aged 84
articles.raw_rss: Sir Ian was one of Scotland’s wealthiest people
articles.raw_meta: Sir Ian was one of Scotland’s wealthiest people
articles.jina_text:
Billionaire Sir Ian Wood, who made his fortune in the North Sea oil industry with the Wood Group company, has died at the age of 84.
Sir Ian was one of Scotland’s wealthiest people.
He studied psychology at Aberdeen University and contemplated a career in academia before taking over the family business in 1967, turning the Aberdeen-based company from a fishing operation into an engineering and consulting giant.
Over the following decades, he formed a separate engineering company servicing the rapidly growing North Sea oil business.





At its height, the Wood Group was valued at more than £5 billion and carried out work in the energy industry around the world.

Sir Ian died peacefully at his home, his family said.





open image in gallery
Sir Ian Wood has died at the age of 84 (PA Archive)
The billionaire previously told The Independent that he found his psychology studies helpful for succeeding in business.
“Business is all about understanding people's motivations. But people often hide their real feelings behind a front,” he said.


He also worked for 16 hours a day for much of his career, was a teetotaller and stayed fit, enjoying squash, tennis, and walking.
In 1984, Aberdeen University awarded him an honorary doctorate in law.
The billionaire, who retired as chair of the group in 2012, was knighted in 1994 for services to the oil and gas industry.



He was later made a member of the Order of the Thistle, Scotland’s highest order of chivalry.
His philanthropic work was carried out through the Wood Foundation, which he founded in 2007.
The foundation is involved in a number of investments and charitable work around agriculture and conservation in east Africa, as well as projects in Scotland.





In 2024, the Sunday Times Rich List ranked Sir Ian and his family in third place on the list of Scotland’s wealthiest people.
The newspaper said that their fortune had increased by £91 million to just over £1.9 billion.

“Sir Ian was a devoted husband, father, grandfather and friend,” a statement from his family said.
“While many knew him as an entrepreneur, philanthropist and one of Scotland’s most influential business leaders, those closest to him will remember above all his kindness, generosity, determination and unwavering commitment to his family.”

articles.raw_content:
Only two years ago, smarting from her expulsion from Sir Keir Starmer’s government, it looked as if Louise Haigh’s political career was over. Now she’s so central to Andy Burnham’s administration she’s the most powerful woman in British politics.



“The whole story of Andy Burnham’s rise has been women either angry with Keir or furious at the boys’ club around him,” a Labour MP said. “Talk about ‘don’t get mad, get even’.”



Sacked by Starmer, Haigh, 40, is now so powerful she helped to choose and interview the candidates for Cabinet positions and even wielded her influence over the pick for Chancellor of the Exchequer, usually the second most influential member of government.





She and ally Anneliese Midgley, the new Chief Whip, who both have strong links to Labour’s union backers, persuaded Burnham that Ed Miliband’s net zero agenda was at risk of costing jobs. MPs had lobbied the pair to block Miliband, worried his environmental zeal could cost votes in Labour’s traditional heartlands, despite his popularity with the party’s grassroots.



Like Burnham, and unlike Miliband, Haigh is a northerner and instinctively suspicious of the London political classes. Alongside Midgely and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, she’s been dubbed one of Burnham’s “northern queens”. During the Makerfield by-election, she took pitches from visiting Cabinet ministers keen to be kept on under the new administration.

Only two years ago, smarting from her expulsion from Sir Keir Starmer’s government, it looked as if Louise Haigh’s political career was over. Now she’s so central to Andy Burnham’s administration she’s the most powerful woman in British politics.



“The whole story of Andy Burnham’s rise has been women either angry with Keir or furious at the boys’ club around him,” a Labour MP said. “Talk about ‘don’t get mad, get even’.”



Sacked by Starmer, Haigh, 40, is now so powerful she helped to choose and interview the candidates for Cabinet positions and even wielded her influence over the pick for Chancellor of the Exchequer, usually the second most influential member of government.





She and ally Anneliese Midgley, the new Chief Whip, who both have strong links to Labour’s union backers, persuaded Burnham that Ed Miliband’s net zero agenda was at risk of costing jobs. MPs had lobbied the pair to block Miliband, worried his environmental zeal could cost votes in Labour’s traditional heartlands, despite his popularity with the party’s grassroots.



Like Burnham, and unlike Miliband, Haigh is a northerner and instinctively suspicious of the London political classes. Alongside Midgely and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, she’s been dubbed one of Burnham’s “northern queens”. During the Makerfield by-election, she took pitches from visiting Cabinet ministers keen to be kept on under the new administration.



Second only to the Prime Minister

At the height of the third heatwave, in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.




[xdelx]




Meanwhile, blazes have wrought destruction in mainland Europe this week, with 220,000 forced out of their homes in south-west France and 116,000 evacuated in Spain.








This comes as a Met Office meteorologist said UK heatwave thresholds will need to be adjusted to take into account the warming climate, which has seen temperature records repeatedly broken this year.




A National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) spokesperson said: “With the Met Office warning that a fourth heatwave could develop this week, bringing another period of very hot weather to parts of the UK, fire and rescue services remain on alert and are continuing to prepare for renewed wildfire risk.”


The National Fire Chiefs Council said most wildfires are preventable (Brian Lawless/PA)
PA Wire




Battling nearly 20 wildfires at once demonstrates “the scale of the challenge posed by the prolonged hot, dry conditions”, they added.




“Most wildfires are preventable and we are asking everyone to play their part in helping to protect our communities, wildlife and natural spaces, while easing the pressure on firefighters who have already faced an exceptionally challenging summer.”




Temperatures cooled, winds picked up and a smattering of rain fell for many during the weekend.




But parts of southern England will yet again meet their heatwave criteria on Wednesday, which could reach highs of 32C or 33C, and more will on Thursday.


Swithland Reservoir in Leicestershire (Joe Giddens/PA)
PA Wire




A yellow heat alert has been issued from 9am on Tuesday to 9am on Friday for the East and West Midlands, the south-east, south-west and east of England, as well as Yorkshire and the Humber.











The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issued a warning of possible “significant impacts” on health and social care services, including a rise in deaths among the elderly or people with health conditions, and an increase in drownings.




Forecasters are expecting this week’s hot spell to be a “north-south split”, with clouds and outbreaks of rain continuing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England.







But the peak will be “almost a blink and you miss it”, with temperatures widely cooling close to average by the weekend, said senior Met Office meteorologist Dan Stroud.




July was 3C above average across the UK, according to provisional Met Office data on the month so far.

What is a ‘fire cloud’, and how have they worsened wildfires in Europe? 




Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux as the forecast of another heatwave threatened to deepen the crisis and the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.
Windy conditions on Saturday night hampered efforts to extinguish the blaze in the Gironde region of south-western France – which has consumed an area four times the size of Paris and caused nearly 220,000 people to be evacuated.

In Spain, fires west of Madrid were being brought under control, but Sánchez spoke on Sunday of “difficult hours”.
Weather forecasters say another heatwave could hit France from Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 40C in some areas.
Wildfires have forced about 375,000 people to flee their homes in France and Spain. In France nearly 260,000 have been forced to flee, while in neighbouring Spain 116,000 have been evacuated this week.

The fire situation in Gironde remained “broadly stable overnight” with no major developments, the local authority said on Monday. “Security and emergency services remain fully mobilised and are continuing their operations on the ground,” the statement said.


Nearly 260,000 people have been evacuated across France as a whole, including 36,000 ordered to leave another wildfire zone in the Landes region farther south earlier this week.

Sophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, which includes the Gironde, said that the highly unpredictable nature of this wildfire was a phenomenon never seen before in France. “I urge tourists not to come to Gironde as long as the fire has not been contained,” she said. “I invite tourists who are already here to think about going to another destination. articles.jina_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron will a hold a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday as wildfires close in on the south-western city of Bordeaux.
Another heatwave is set to complicate efforts to tackle the expanding blaze, which is about 15km (9 miles) from Bordeaux, mayor Thomas Cazenave said. Earlier he said there were no plans to evacuate the population of about 850,000.
Wildfires have raged across Europe over the past week, primarily in France and Spain, where more than 330,000 people have been evacuated across both countries.
Macron said on Saturday that France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".
Tens of thousands of people have already been evacuated from Bordeaux's surrounding region, with France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez saying the situation remained "very unfavourable" and the fire was "moving erratically" towards the city.
Weather forecasts for the country warned that temperatures could spike to 40C in some areas from Tuesday.




Image source, Lorena Sopena Lopez/Anadolu via Getty Image




France's main fire in the Gironde region has caused an unprecedented "pyrocumulonimbus" - a giant fire thunderstorm fuelled by its own winds and lightning, said the National Firefighters Federation of France (FNSPF). 
"We don't know how the blaze will spread, the fire front is constantly shifting. We cannot fight it directly," said spokesman Eric Brocardi.
"It's a David-versus-Goliath scenario." 
He added that to control the blaze, it would need to rain "heavily for three days" or require firefighters steering it towards a place where it can die down on its own, like the sea.
The wildfires have badly affected France. About 42,000 hectares have been burnt in the south-west, in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. Since the start of the year, about 98,000 hectares have been scorched.
More than 220,000 people have been evacuated in the south-west of the country.









Meanwhile, firefighters in Spain battled a new blaze on Sunday near the eastern coastal city of Valencia where around 15,000 people have been forced to flee their homes.
Pilar Bernabe, the central government's delegate to Valencia, said the fire had been "very intense" and weather conditions were expected to worsen.
Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, who is expected to visit affected areas in Valencia on Monday, said the fires were advancing slowly.
"Difficult hours lie ahead," said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez during a visit to the fire zone in Ávila province, west of Madrid. 
He also called for "a major public pact on the climate emergency".
Spain's King Felipe VI said the wildfires had caused "incalculable" damage to the country's natural heritage, as he toured an emergency shelter in Villamanta, south-west of the capital.

Every new UK home should have air conditioning, say Liberal Democrats


Exclusive: Party says housing stock ‘woefully unprepared’ for extreme heat and new rules for builders must be set




All new UK homes should be built with air conditioning to cope with the effects of the climate crisis, according to the Liberal Democrats.
The party says British homes are dangerously unsuited to rising temperatures, meaning passive cooling measures such as planting more trees in residential areas are necessary.

The Lib Dems also want air conditioning to be mandatory in essential public buildings such as schools and health facilities.
The problem of overwarm homes has been highlighted by a UK Health Protection Agency yellow alert for high temperatures to run from Tuesday morning until Friday morning for the south-east, south-west and east of England, the Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.



Temperatures in London are forecast to reach 32C (90F) on Wednesday, before cooling. Some other parts of the UK will be wet with notably lower temperatures.
As well as being hot, much of the summer has been exceptionally dry. In July so far, there has been just 5% of the average rainfall across England, falling to 1% in the south, bringing droughts and severe risk of wildfires.







My homemade air-con unit does the trick | Letters 

Read more
The Lib Dems’ “climate ready” programme would make it a legal requirement for new homes to have either air conditioning or another cooling system. They say this is especially important for older people or those in poor health.
The number of UK homes with air conditioning has doubled in the past three years amid rising temperatures, according to industry estimates. However, this still comes to only about 4m of the estimated 30m-plus homes in the country.
According to polling commissioned by the Lib Dems, 28% of people said they had bought a fan or an air conditioning unit during the recent heatwaves, with 26% of respondents saying the conditions had left them feeling unwell or faint.


Tim Farron, the party’s environment spokesperson, said: “This latest set of relentless heatwaves has taught us that Britain is woefully unprepared for extreme heat, and families across Britain are paying for the cost of inaction.
“With another heatwave on the horizon, the government must step in with a new plan that takes the onus off already-struggling Brits and commits developers to build homes fit for the future – insulated properly and equipped with air conditioning.”

Ed Miliband indicates development and climate will be at heart of UK foreign policy


Exclusive: Foreign secretary to take up World Bank seat and play active role in shaping changes to global lender 




Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.
The position, which is usually delegated to a junior minister, means Miliband will play an active role in shaping the changes to the World Bank that developing countries have called for, and ensuring the climate remains a core focus for overseas aid.

Miliband, who was energy and net zero secretary under Keir Starmer, will say: “International development is not an add-on to British foreign policy – it is central to it. By taking on the role of UK governor to the World Bank, I want to send an unambiguous signal that this government is serious about its global leadership on development and climate.”
His announcement comes as fires continue to devastate swathes of France and Spain, and after Scotland called for military aid to tackle a blaze that engulfed the Cairngorms. Conditions approaching drought across England and parts of Wales have prompted hosepipe bans, and the heatwave that swept across Europe in June is estimated to have cost the continent’s grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.
By taking up the World Bank seat personally, Miliband is sending a clear signal that while other politicians even now argue against net zero policies, the Foreign Office will continue to drive climate action.
The move comes at a crucial time for the international lender, which has come under heavy pressure from the Trump administration to reverse a previous focus on climate finance. Last month, the publicly funded bank scrapped its goal for 45% of its finance to be directed to climate-related ends.
Experts welcomed Miliband’s decision as a boost to climate action. Lord Stern, a professor of economics at the London School of Economics, said the foreign secretary’s take-up of the UK governor’s seat would “send a powerful and important signal” to the world.
“As a former chief economist and senior vice-president of the World Bank, I know that the UK can punch above its weight,” he said. “But only if the leadership is there from the top. In recent years, that has slipped. Ed Miliband will be restoring development and climate to the priority in our international relationships that they must have, in a world facing climate and biodiversity crises, and with real and growing threats to the wellbeing of the world’s poorest.”

‘Scandalous, irrational and irresponsible’: French beekeepers’ fury at lifting of pesticides ban


Allowing use of two neonicotinoids to combat crop-ruining disease will kill bees and reduce harvests, union says




Beekeepers and environmentalists in France have reacted furiously after parliament approved a bill reauthorising two banned pesticides scientists say can poison bees.
“There are no words to describe the frustration,” said Carolyn Bouguet, a beekeeper in Essonne, greater Paris. “Bee populations have already been badly compromised by climate change, new parasites and loss of habitat. And now this.”

Henri Clément, a beekeeper in the southern Lozère department and spokesperson for the French beekeeping association, UNAF, said the measure was “an absolute disaster for our sector, and for biodiversity as a whole”.
For bees, the risk was “very high mortality rates and reduced harvests”, Clément told local media. “It’s just incomprehensible these pesticides have been reauthorised. We’ve been fighting them for 30 years. It’s scandalous, irrational and irresponsible.”


The law, passed on Tuesday, allows France’s food and environmental safety agency, Anses, to grant waivers authorising the use of the pesticides acetamiprid and flupyradifurone in struggling farm sectors and under exceptional circumstances.
The use of the pesticides, allowed in the EU but banned in France, will be authorised to combat aphid-borne diseases that can ruin crops of sugar beet, apples, hazelnuts and cherries, which has led producers to claim they can no longer compete with European rivals.
Scientific studies have established that acetamiprid, a neonicotinoid with powerful neurotoxic effects, can poison bees, affecting their foraging capacity and memory. A 2024 study suggested flupyradifurone could be lethal to some honeybees.
Greenpeace France said the country’s centrist government and its rightwing allies in parliament were “trampling on science, health, the environment and the clear will of the people”, describing the legislation as “deeply concerning” and “a disgrace”.
France’s environment minister, Monique Barbut, said the legislation was “one environmental setback too many” and submitted her resignation on Wednesday, but was later persuaded to stay on after meeting President Emmanuel Macron.

Jeremy Clarkson has issued a dire warning (Picture: Matthew Vincent/PA Wire)



Jeremy Clarkson has delivered a grim assessment of British farming, admitting he deliberately left hundreds of acres at Diddly Squat untouched this year because growing crops would have guaranteed him a financial loss.

The former Top Gear presenter, who has spent the past seven years running his Oxfordshire farm and documenting the highs and lows in Clarkson’s Farm, said making money from growing food has become ‘quite simply impossible’.

Writing in his column for The Sun, the 66-year-old warned that the situation is only likely to deteriorate.

‘Action is needed now because farmers have reached the point where it is quite simply impossible to make money from growing food,’ he wrote.

‘This year, I have 200 acres on my farm where we grew nothing at all. We knew that if we planted it with wheat or barley, we would definitely make a loss.’

Clarkson believes the outlook will become even bleaker next year, claiming the introduction of a Net Zero carbon tax on fertiliser will pile further pressure on an industry already struggling to stay afloat.

He suggested farmers may soon have little choice but to abandon traditional food production in favour of more profitable alternatives.

New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea


Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence




Production at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.
Andy Burnham’s new government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despite opposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.

Rosebank, located about 80 miles north-west of Shetland, was believed to be ready to generate oil before the end of the year, pending ministerial approval.
Adura, the company responsible for Rosebank, now says it anticipates this will happen at some point in 2027. The field is projected to produce 300m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifespan, according to industry estimates.


Some MPs believe enhanced domestic production of oil and gas would help tackle the cost of living, a central focus of the new prime minister, by improving energy security amid global instability, while green campaigners believe the impact on the UK economy of exploiting the fields would be minimal.
However, delays at Rosebank mean production at the field will be unlikely to affect the UK’s energy supply over the winter months. Licences for Rosebank and another site, Jackdaw, were granted under the Conservatives but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups.
The new energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on the fields’ future after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in August.







North Sea oil industry urges Burnham to approve new drilling in UK waters

Read more
Earlier this week, Adura told the BBC that the Jackdaw site, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could produce gas as early as October.
However, preparations for oil production at Rosebank have been hindered by the rig incident, which occurred on 18 April. No workers were hurt, but two central pieces of drilling equipment, including a safety valve, were dropped 1,100 metres on to the seabed.


The platform, hired by Adura from Norwegian company Odfjell Drilling, was taken to a shipyard in Bergen for repairs. It is now back at Rosebank but not yet operational.
Odfjell Drilling said in internal documentation that the rig could be out of action for up to four months. The Guardian understands this means that some oil wells will be completed significantly behind schedule.

articles.title: UK set for fourth heatwave as wildfires hit parts of country
articles.raw_rss: The UK has had 20% of its average July rainfall.
articles.raw_meta: The UK has had 20% of its average July rainfall.
articles.jina_text:
People play cricket on a lone patch of green grass surrounded by parched land at Victoria Park in east London (Ben Whitley/PA)
PA Wire



Pol Allingham
3 minutes ago







A fourth heatwave is expected to hit the UK as wildfires tear through parts of the country.




Homes were evacuated as a blaze swept through the Cairngorms National Park in what Police Scotland declared as a major incident, and emergency crews continued to tackle wildfires in Wales.




North Wales and the Upper Severn became the first part of the UK to declare drought status on Thursday, and parts of Exeter, Devon and Usk in Wales met their heatwave thresholds for 20 consecutive days.








No rain has fallen in July in Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire and West Sussex, and 16 counties have recorded 0.1mm, which “might just be a bit of dew on the grass”, said the Met Office’s senior operational meteorologist Marco Petagna.




The UK has had 20% of its average July rainfall, which takes into account the wetter areas.




It is “very, very unusual” for a hot and dry spell to last this long, Mr Petagna added.




The dry conditions follow last year’s drought summer, as the UK faces more extreme weather fuelled by human-caused climate change, mostly from burning fossil fuels.




Heat alerts are in place across parts of England with officials warning that temperatures are likely to impact on health and wellbeing.




Yellow alerts for the East Midlands, East of England, London, South East, South West and West Midlands are in place until 9am on Sunday.


A wildfire burning in the Cairngorms National Park (RSPB Scotland/PA)
PA Media




Cooler and fresher weather is expected widely on Sunday, ending the longest running heatwaves with highs of 25C and 26C possible in the South East and high teens and low 20s more widely elsewhere.











But the heat will climb again at start of the week, with Monday’s high forecast at 27C in the South East, just below the area’s heatwave threshold of 28C.




Heatwave thresholds will start to be topped the following day, with highs of more than 30C expected until Thursday in the South East.







Next week’s heatwave may not be the last of the summer, the Met Office’s long range forecast suggests.




“(The weather) is a bit more changeable in the short term, but as we head more into August there are hints that conditions will settle down and become drier again”, Mr Petagna said.




Wildfires continue to burn across the Rhinogydd mountains, North Wales, and Blaenavon, South Wales, with the latter affecting 220 hectares.

articles.title: Fossil fuels in Australia receive four times more government support than renewables, report finds
articles.raw_rss: The report comes months before Australia takes charge of negotiations at this year's United Nations climate summit Cop31
articles.raw_meta: The report comes months before Australia takes charge of negotiations at this year
articles.jina_text:
Australia is spending more than four times as much supporting fossil fuels as it does renewable energy, according to a report that warns the country risks losing tens of billions of pounds in export earnings by trying to be both a green superpower and a major coal and gas supplier.
The report comes months before the country takes charge of negotiations at this year's United Nations climate summit. 
Governments in Australia provide an estimated A$20.1bn (about £9.9bn) a year in support to fossil fuels, against A$4.6bn (about £2.3bn) for renewable energy, according to Energy Crossroads, published by WWF-Australia.





The figures cover subsidies, tax concessions, and direct spending at federal and state level.
Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at Cop31, which runs from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye, under an unusual arrangement in which Türkiye hosts the conference and holds the formal presidency while Australia manages the talks, prepares draft texts and issues the summit's cover decision.

The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, will lead the negotiations.

The report argues that the country’s split approach, which it calls a hedge, is neither neutral nor prudent, because green and fossil industries compete for the same capital, policy attention and infrastructure.


Analysis prepared for the report by the consultancy Cyan Ventures estimates that Australia could lose up to A$70bn (about £34bn) in fossil fuel export value by 2035 as demand across Asia shifts towards renewables.
"Australia is pulling in two directions at once," said Rob Law, WWF-Australia's senior manager for energy transition.



"We can no longer afford to position ourselves as a renewable energy partner while simultaneously propping up and expanding fossil fuel production. This sends mixed signals to investors, undermines Australia's credibility as a trade partner and creates space for others to lead."

 ‘No time to waste’: Greece bids for Mount Olympus to be included on Unesco list of world heritage sites


Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation




More than four decades have elapsed since Evangelos Geroliolios made his first ascent to the home of the ancient gods. At the top of Mount Olympus, on the rocky peak of Greece’s highest mountain, he felt unalloyed awe.
“I’ve never forgotten that unique moment, that unique feeling up there on the throne of Zeus,” recalled Geroliolios, who as mayor of Dion-Olympus now spends a great deal of his time administering the area around the site.

Described by Homer as the “seat of the immortals”, its craggy summit – where Zeus, the father of the gods, is said to have held court – rises 2,918 metres above the sea.
“You get this incredible sense of place, fused by myth, beauty and the weight of history – all of which we want to share and hope will be recognised internationally,” he said.


Greek officials have long lobbied for Mount Olympus to be included on the Unesco list of world heritage sites; soon champions of the cause will learn if the site will finally be granted the coveted designation.
The World Heritage Committee is scheduled to begin discussing the nomination on Sunday at its 48th session, now under way in Busan, South Korea. The annual meeting ends on 29 July.
Greece first proposed the mountain’s inclusion on the list of places considered by Unesco to be “of outstanding value to humanity” in 2014, citing both its cultural and environmental significance.
The area was declared a national forest – the country’s first – in 1938, in tribute to the uniqueness of terrain covered not only by verdant forest but alpine fields, gorges, ravines and springs, all within close proximity of the sea.
Litochoro, the nearest town to the mountain, lies three miles (5km) away from breathtaking beaches practically at the foot of the mountain.
In recognition of its abundance of flora and fauna, Unesco designated Olympus a biosphere reserve in 1981. Further environmental protection came in the form of a presidential decree, when the mountain was declared a national park, in 2021.

articles.raw_rss: Residents feared air pollution, water contamination and noise in latest pushback against AI data center boom
articles.raw_meta: Residents feared air pollution, water contamination and noise in latest pushback against AI data center boom
articles.jina_text:
As the artificial intelligence boom continues, there have been new environmental concerns about data centers popping up in communities. The latest fight is between the Nashville Zoo, a 188-acre park just 6 miles south of downtown, and data center provider DC Blox.
DC Blox wants to build a 69,200-square-foot data center next to the zoo with landscape buffers and concrete walls to separate the two areas.




Amid backlash from locals, DC Blox proposed a memorandum of understanding with the Nashville Zoo that would have created the data center, but zoo officials declined, local media reported Thursday.
The 69,200 square-foot structure included in the MOU is less than the size initially proposed, and DC Blox also offered to return some of the land it purchased back to the zoo for future development, reports said.






open image in gallery
The Nashville Zoo has rejected a deal that would have allowed a new data center near the animal park as nationwide protests against data centers, like one pictured in California, ramp up across the country (AFP via Getty Images)
“We will not turn out backs on the 563,000 members of this community and beyond who have supported us, nor the 3,000 animals entrusted to our care,” Nashville Zoo CEO Rick Schwartz said in a statement.


“We stand by what we've said from the beginning: a data center this close to vulnerable species, schools, and neighboring communities has not been proven safe,” he said.
Locals who oppose the data center warned of air pollution, water contamination and noise. 
“We’re worried about noise. We’re worried about what it’s going to do to the zoo. The list just keeps going and going and going, so it’s hard to pick like one thing that we’re worried about,” resident Drew Small told WKRN last month. “It’s all of it — it’s our creeks, it’s our breathing air, it’s our drinking water, it’s our electricity.”


Resident Will Thomsen told WTVF, “I'm worried now that I have to watch the quality of our water because of the effects that data centers have on water. 
“I’m worried about their noise,” he said. I’m worried about the impact on my neighbors and the animals at the zoo.”





open image in gallery
Locals pushed back on the data center, warning of air pollution, water contamination and noise (Getty Images)
DC Blox writes on its website that they will commit to a sound level no greater than 65 dB(A) at the property line, which it says is “within the general range of ambient sound levels in the area.”




"DC Blox remains committed to finding a mutually beneficial outcome for this project,” a company spokesperson said in a statement shared by WTVF. 
“Along with considering the size and scope, the project will include design elements such as sound mitigation, buffers and barriers so there is not an impact on the zoo or local neighbors.”
The Independent has reached out to DC Blox and the Nashville Zoo for comment.

articles.raw_content:
Readers discuss Burnham’s first moves as PM, how good the new Odyssey film really is and whether we’re actually in a cost-of-living crisis (Picture: Toby Melville / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)



Do you agree with our readers? Have your say on these MetroTalk topics and more in the comments

		
			
				Is removing VAT from domestic energy bills a good move?			
			
				Andy Burnham’s first attempt to ease the cost-of-living crisis as prime minister – by removing VAT from domestic electricity bills (Metro, Wed) – may be popular but is, from the point of view of economics, wrong-headed.
Economics and experience tell us price is determined by supply and demand.
Energy prices have increased because supply has been restricted due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. If the price we pay is reduced by the tax cut, demand will rise, putting upward pressure again on price.
Thus the net effect of the tax cut will be, at least to a degree, to transfer money which would have gone to the government to the energy companies.
A tax increase, conversely, reduces demand and so depresses the market price, so that, in effect, part of the tax is borne by the energy companies rather than the consumer. Bernard Winchester, Norwood
			
		
		

‘Inflation is down’ so is there no cost-of-living crisis?

We keep reading about the ‘cost-of-living crisis’ but inflation is down to 2.6 per cent. In 1975, soon after I had married, it hit 25 per cent. Let’s get some perspective! Jami

Explainer
How dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?


The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk




Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people across southern Europe to flee their homes, while powerful infernos across Canada and the US choke big cities with thick smoke.


How deadly are wildfires?
Wildfires directly kill hundreds of people each year. Though they may seem apocalyptic, the death toll is far lower than from floods, which kill thousands, and from heatwaves, which kill hundreds of thousands.
But when you factor in smoke, the human cost rises rapidly. The latest study estimates that the air pollution spewed by wildfires kills a staggering 1.5 million people each year. The toxic fumes can reach so far that tendrils of smoke from Australian bushfires have menaced South America, while smoke from Canadian fires – which regularly suffocate cities across the US – have fouled the air in Europe. Last year, a study attributed 22,000 early deaths in Europe to Canadian wildfire smoke in 2023, out of a total of 82,000 deaths.

What causes wildfires?
Many things can spark a wildfire: natural causes such as lightning, faulty infrastructure such as downed power lines, or people behaving badly. Devastating blazes in recent years have been started by smokers tossing cigarette butts, tourists failing to put out campfires, and even arsonists intentionally setting nature alight.
But whether those sparks turn into small fires or raging blazes depends on the weather. Fires need hot, dry fuel to burn, and they spread further with strong winds.

How does climate breakdown affect wildfires?
Fossil fuel pollution has heated the planet by about 1.3C, raising the risk of prolonged heat that turns forests and grasslands into tinderboxes. In some regions, such as the Mediterranean, global heating is also fuelling droughts that dry out lush greenery.
Scientists have found that such shifts have made the wildfires that have happened this year in places including California, South Korea and Australia more likely – in some cases doubling the chance of extreme weather conditions that help fires spread.

Are wildfires getting worse?

The calcium content in carrots fell by more than a quarter between the mid-1970s and the late 1990s, according to the US Department of Agriculture. Photograph: Marcio José Sánchez/AP


Nutrients in our food are declining. Can regenerative agriculture save it?


Approach focuses on rebuilding soil health, increasing biodiversity and restoring natural ecosystems




For the last few decades, the nutrient content of our crops has been declining. In the late 90s, the US Department of Agriculture found the vitamin C content of lemons had decreased by almost a third over the previous 22 years. Calcium in carrots, an important source especially for non-meat eaters, had reduced, on average, by more than a quarter. Vitamin A in bananas was down by 57%. The mineral content of wheat has declined by between 20-30% since the 1960s.
A number of reasons have been suggested for this worrying decline, ranging from new varieties of crop that are bred to grow quicker and bigger to the higher carbon dioxide levels in the air causing plants to produce more sugars and starches (they grow faster but they produce fewer nutrients). A wide range of fixes have been suggested, from GM crops to synthetic soil amendments, or underground farms.



One group of agricultural researchers, however, argues that the answer to declining nutrients may be more straightforward than that: regenerative agriculture. This “focuses on building organic matter and ecosystems in the soil”, says Francesca Brkic. “The question is, does that therefore deliver more nutrition?”
Her work, in conjunction with the University of Lincoln, explores how regenerative agriculture affects nutrient density. The researchers sampled a number of products and found that iron in kale could be up to 22 times higher in samples from regenerative farms compared with conventional ones, while selenium (an antioxidant) in dried peas was eight times higher and folate (good for red blood cells) in carrots was up to 20,000 times greater.
Brkic says: “Organic had to be our minimum baseline, because regen doesn’t have a certifiable standard. But while organic as a concept focuses on not doing harmful things, it doesn’t specify that you are doing positive things.” Regenerative farms, in this case, were defined by those using cover crops and grazing animals, while abstaining from ploughing the land and using insecticides or other pesticides.

Fungicide and insecticide are sprayed on a field of bell pepper plants in Florida. Photograph: Design Pics Inc/Alamy
The way soil is treated by modern farming may be part of the problem. Ploughing and heavy use of chemicals – fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides – disturb and even destroy the soil’s mycorrhizal networks, which we are only just coming to under

Scientists decry Trump’s ‘blame game’ after he claims Canada ‘poisoning’ US air


Trump told Mark Carney ‘you got to stop these fires from coming in’ as experts say wildfires symptom of climate crisis





Scientists have reacted with incredulity after Donald Trump accused Canada of “poisoning” the US’s air with smoke billowing from a slew of forest fires and threatened sanctions upon the country’s northern neighbor.
The US president has said that he raised the issue of smoke wafting into the US from nearly 1,000 Canadian wildfires with Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, at the weekend’s World Cup final.

“I told him, you got to stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air,” Trump said. “If we can help them, we’ll help them. But maybe they should pay us some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs.”
Trump, who has previously advocated the “raking” and “cleaning” of forests to prevent major conflagrations, this week announced 50% tariffs upon Canada, a long-term US ally that he has previously threatened with annexation. The US is being “unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air”, Trump claimed last week.
With palls of wildfire smoke causing unhealthy, hazy skies in cities including New York, Washington DC, Detroit and Toronto in recent weeks, some Republicans in Congress have issued further threats against Canada. Bernie Moreno, a Republican senator from Ohio, said he will introduce legislation to sanction Canada for the “atrocity” of not managing its forests properly.


View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump walks ahead of Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum and Canada’s Mark Carney at the World Cup final in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on 19 June. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images
Such threats have been met with shock in Canada, where thousands of people have been evacuated from fires that have badly burned remote towns. More than 8.1m acres (3.3m hectares) have been consumed by fires across Canada’s vast, mostly unpopulated boreal forests, a steep increase on the long-term average.


Such fierce wildfires are a symptom of the climate crisis rather than a lack of management, experts warn, with the current blazes worsened by the recent severe heat dome that expanded from the US into Canada. The world is rapidly heating up due to the burning of fossil fuels, a process that Trump has actively sought to accelerate.
